newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Alusuisse profit rises, sees better 97.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Alusuisse profit rises, sees better 97.

text.p: Alusuisse-Lonza Holding AG, the Swiss diversified industrial group, said on Tuesday that 1996 net profit rose eight percent to 417 million Swiss francs ($292 million) and it was confident that profits would rise further this year.
Chairman Hans Jucker said Alusuisse was very satisfied with the 1996 profits because they were earned in a tough economic environment, especially in Europe.
The profit was below most analysts' forecasts and Alusuisse shares were down 14 francs at 1,196 francs during early afternoon on the Swiss Exchange.
"The results could have disappointed some investors," one share trader said.
Alusuisse's 1996 sales rose seven percent to 8.0 billion francs with major gains from the packaging division, which saw strong growth from its acquisition of Wheaton Inc. of the United States.

Despite the profit gain, Alusuisse will keep its dividend steady at 18.75 francs per share in the light of planned capital investments of more than 800 million francs this year, up from 700 million in 1996.
Among this year's investments are a chemical plant in Singapore, an alumimium smelter in Iceland and modernisation of Wheaton's glass packaging facilities.
In 1996 Alusuisse spent almost 600 million francs in buying Wheaton, a U.S. packaging company, and Celltech Biologics Ltd., a biotechnology group.
Operating profit in 1996 also rose eight percent to 702 milllion francs with margins up to 9.6 percent from 9.5 percent.
"For 1997, we again expect an improvement in the group results compared with 1996," Theodor Tschopp, chief executive of Alusuisse, told news conference.
Chief financial officer Sergio Marchionne, designated to become chief executive in April, said that a substantial amount of investments were of a medium- to long-term nature.
The impact of these investments would therefore be visible on earnings only by 1998 at the earliest, he added.
Marchionne declined to be drawn on his strategic vision for Alusuisse and whether the company would continue to rest on its three pillars of chemicals, packaging and aluminium.

Alusuisse also put its weight behind efforts to clear up the dispute between Switzerland and many Jewish organisations about the whereabouts of funds deposited with Swiss banks before and during World War Two.
Jucker said Alusuisse would contribute generously to a Holocaust memorial fund and encouraged the Swiss government to act quickly in joining a fund set up by banks.
On Sunday business executives met the Swiss National Bank (SNB) and Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti and agreed they were ready to contribute to a humanitarian fund.
Switzerland's three biggest banks, under fire from critics about their role in the war, have set up a 100 million Swiss franc fund for a Holocaust memorial fund.
The banks have been accused by Jewish organisations, Holocaust survivors and their families that they hoarded assets of victims of Nazism placed with them for safekeeping during the war.
The government has said it is working at full speed on the guidelines for a fund it may later join.
The government says it would decide whether and how much to pay only after a panel of international historians presented its first findings on Switzerland's wartime role as a financial centre.
Joining other critics of the government's position, Jucker said legal questions really were not the main issue here, but rather "quick humanitarian action that can help in an uncomplicated way".
-- Zurich Editorial +41 1 631 7340 ($ = 1.429 Swiss Francs)
